subject: operating-systems
title: The system-call interface
summary: System calls let a process request OS services such as file I/O, process creation, and interprocess communication.

resources.title: intro(2): Introduction to system calls
resources.why: Explains kernel entry points, library wrappers, mode transitions, and error reporting.

resources.title: syscalls(2): Linux system calls
resources.why: Lists system calls and explains their role as the application-to-kernel interface.

questions.prompt: Which POSIX-like function requests bytes from an open file descriptor?
options: read()
strlen()
qsort()
strcmp()
questions.answerKey: read() requests data from a file descriptor; the other functions operate on strings or arrays in user space.
questions.explanation: read() is the file-descriptor I/O operation in this list.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a C library function from a system call?
options: Every system call runs only in user mode
A library wrapper may invoke a system call, while many library functions run entirely in user space
System calls can only sort arrays
Every library function has its own system-call number
questions.answerKey: Wrappers often prepare arguments and enter the kernel, but functions such as strlen() usually compute in user space.
questions.explanation: A function call is not necessarily a system call.

questions.prompt: On a POSIX-like system, a program wants to create a child and then replace the child's program image. Which sequence is conventional?
options: malloc() followed by free()
printf() followed by fflush()
fork() followed by an exec-family call
strlen() followed by strcmp()
questions.answerKey: fork() creates a child process; an exec-family call replaces the calling process's program image.
questions.explanation: String and memory-management functions do not create a child process.

questions.prompt: A program calls strlen("hello") and then read(fd, buf, 5). Which statement is correct on a typical Unix-like system?
options: strlen() reads from the disk and read() counts characters in memory
Both must enter kernel mode because both are C functions
Neither can return a result
strlen() can inspect local memory in user space; read() requests OS-managed I/O
questions.answerKey: strlen() ordinarily scans the process's own memory; read() asks the OS to read from a file descriptor.
questions.explanation: The distinction is local computation versus a request for an operating-system service.

questions.prompt: Why is directly dereferencing a guessed disk-controller address not a general replacement for read(fd, buf, n)?
options: It makes all storage devices expose identical registers
It bypasses file abstractions, permission checks, and device coordination
It guarantees the file descriptor is always valid
It automatically provides portable error handling
questions.answerKey: The OS uses file descriptors and drivers to validate access and coordinate devices; direct hardware access is protected and device-specific.
questions.explanation: A file descriptor is an OS-managed handle, not a physical device address.

questions.prompt: Give one system-call example for file I/O, one for process management, and one for interprocess communication. State the service each requests.
questions.answerKey: Examples: read() or write() for file-descriptor I/O; fork(), execve(), or waitpid() for process management; pipe() or socket() for interprocess communication. Each name must be paired with the service it requests.

rubric.criterion: Clear distinction between call and service

questions.explanation: Accept other correct OS-specific examples when the purpose is accurately stated.
